ety.text: From Middle English dew, from Old English dēaw (“dew”), from Proto-West Germanic *dauw, from Proto-Germanic *dawwaz, *dawwą (“dew, moisture”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze”). Cognate with German Tau, Dutch dauw and Afrikaans dou. Doublet of dag.
From Middle English dewe, dewen, from Old English *dēawian, from Proto-West Germanic *dauwēn, from Proto-Germanic *dawwāną. Cognates include Saterland Frisian daue, German tauen and Dutch dauwen.

senses.d: Any moisture from the atmosphere condensed by cool bodies upon their surfaces.
Moisture in the air that settles on plants, etc in the morning or evening, resulting in drops.
ex: As therefore the morning devv, is a pavvne of the evenings fatneſſe, ſo, O Lord, let this daies comfort be the earneſt of to morrowes, […]

senses.d: An instance of such moisture settling on plants, etc.
ex: There was a heavy dew this morning.

senses.d: Anything that falls lightly and in a refreshing manner.
An emblem of morning, or fresh vigour.
To wet with, or as if with, dew; to moisten.
ex: The grasses grew / A little ranker since they dewed them so.
Yesterday she tied Kenneth to a tree and left him there for hours when it was dewing.
Withdraw heat from a gas, and it will dew into a liquid. Subtract more heat, and a solid forms.

grp.label: moisture in the air that settles on plants, etc

fr:rosée.gl: dew (moisture in the air that settles on plants, etc)

ety.text: Inherited from Old French rosee, rousee, rosede, from a Vulgar Latin *rōsāta (“dew, mist”), from Latin rōs (“dew, moisture”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rṓs.

Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *rōsāta, from Latin rōs, but borrowed, at least in the form rugiada, from some Gallo-Italic language. The form in question is first documented in the late thirteenth century, as are both of the more indigenous-looking variants above.

es:rocío.gl: dew (moisture on cool surfaces that condenses from the surrounding moist air)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish rucio, or deverbal from rociar, from Vulgar Latin *rōscidare, from Latin rōscidus (“filled with dew”), from rōs (“dew”).

es:sereno.gl: cold humidity in the air that is typical of the night hours

ety.text: Unknown. Cognate with Galician orballo, Asturian orbayu and dialectal Spanish urbajo, orvayo.

pt:riço.gl: a type of curly woollen cloth

ety.text: From Latin ēricius (“hedgehog”). Cognate with Italian riccio, Spanish rizo. Doublet of erício.
